e.etymology: A short form of Columbus, a common given name in 19th-century America. Radio listeners knew it from Lum and Abner, a rural comedy that ran from 1931 to 1954.
From Old Norse Erlendr, a byname from the word for foreign. Swedish and Norwegian immigrants brought it to America.
The Swedish surname of aviator Charles Lindbergh, from lind, linden tree, and berg, hill or mountain. Boys were given it after his solo Atlantic flight in 1927, the name's peak year.

assoc.t: Charles Lindbergh, first to fly the Atlantic solo

e.etymology: The standard written abbreviation of Robert in 19th-century records, entered as if it were the name itself. Robert is Germanic, from hrod, fame, and beraht, bright.
A respelling of Ethel, from Old English aethel, noble, first a short form of names such as Etheldreda and Ethelinda.
An old American spelling of Elijah, Hebrew Eliyahu, my God is Yahweh, the name of the Old Testament prophet.
A variant of Tremaine, a Cornish surname and place name from tre, settlement, and men, stone. The -maine ending was popular in the 1970s and 1980s alongside Jermaine.
A spelling of Hazel, from the Old English name of the hazel tree. It joined the fashion for plant names around 1900.
The eighth letter of the Greek alphabet, used as a girls' name in the early 1900s alongside Alpha, Delta and Zeta.

assoc.t: Greek letter, familiar from sorority and fraternity names

e.etymology: A Japanese girls' name ending in ko, child. The first part depends on the kanji; harmony or peace is the most common reading, and another spelling means first child.
A short form of Pleasant, the English word used as a virtue-style name for boys in the 19th-century South.
An old English pet form of Dorothy, older than Dolly. The toy took its name from the nickname, not the other way around.
e.note: Reads as the toy, or as a dated term of endearment.

assoc.t: doll, the toy; also a term of endearment

e.etymology: Nora with the -etta ending, in the pattern of Loretta and Coretta.
An Anglo-Norman surname meaning son of Hugh, borne by an old Virginia family. In the South it often honored Fitzhugh Lee, the cavalry general who became governor of Virginia.
The title used as a given name. In old British and American folk custom a seventh son, believed to have a gift for healing, was sometimes named Doctor.
e.note: Reads as a professional title, so expect confusion on forms and introductions.

e.etymology: The English surname of Calvin Coolidge, given to boys while he was president. Its peak year, 1924, is the year he won election in his own right.
An old Finnish word for love, used as a girls' name since the 19th century. Finnish immigrants brought it to the upper Midwest.
A surname used as a given name. A well-known bearer was Admiral Robley D. Evans, who led the Great White Fleet out in 1907, a year before the name's peak.
A spelling of Betsy, the pet form of Elizabeth, from Hebrew Elisheva, my God is an oath. This form is used mostly by Spanish-speaking families in the United States.
The Italian form of the Germanic name Emmerich, whose second part means ruler. America is named for the Florentine navigator Amerigo Vespucci.
namesakes: Amerigo Vespucci (Italian navigator for whom America is named)

assoc.t: Amerigo Vespucci, explorer America is named for

e.etymology: A Scottish surname from a pet form of William. Its 1940 peak in the US tracks the presidential run of Wendell Willkie, who spelled the name with two l's.
namesakes: Wilkie Collins (Victorian novelist of The Woman in White and The Moonstone)

e.etymology: An Americanized spelling of Finnish Vaino, short for Vainamoinen, the wise singer-hero of the Kalevala epic. The root word means a wide, slow stretch of river.
German Gott, God, and lieb, dear or love. It was coined by German Protestants in the 17th century as a translation of the Greek name Theophilus.
A Frisian and Low German short form of Herman, from Germanic hari, army, and man. Dutch and north German immigrants brought it to the Midwest.
e.note: Identical to the English word harm.

assoc.t: harm, the word for injury or damage

e.etymology: The Finnish word for worth or value, used as a boys' name in Finland and Estonia. Finnish immigrants brought it to the upper Midwest.
Alexander cut short: the form shows up in late-1980s birth records where the full name ran past a character limit. Alexander is Greek Alexandros, defender of men.
